abstract: Clubroot disease, caused by the obligate biotrophic protist Plasmodiophora brassicae, threatens Brassica crops worldwide. Novel pathogen virulence frequently breaks resistance in agricultural crops, and yet explanations for isolate evolution remain unknown. We combined whole genome sequencing of 192 isolates from 24 countries with a pangenome analysis of 55 high-quality complete or nearly complete genome assemblies and performed functional effector analyses to investigate potential mechanisms of virulence emergence. Three major phylogenetic clusters were identified, including two highly clonal lineages with contrasting virulence profiles, and a genetically diverse population retaining signatures of recombination. Our findings support a model in which genome-wide purifying selection maintained core genome integrity, while effector genes evolved under less constraint. Despite a compact closed pangenome, we identified chromosome 17 as a major hotspot of single nucleotide and structural variations, transposable elements and expansion of ankyrin repeat effectors. Within the variable chromosome 17, PbAnk2 alleles from virulent and avirulent isolates encoded proteins with distinct predicted structures. PbAnk2 interacted with the Arabidopsis co-chaperone DJC31 in yeast two-hybrid and BiFC assays, whereas co-immunoprecipitation did not detect an interaction for the allele found in isolates that break CRa-mediated resistance, suggesting that allelic variation may alter PbAnk2's association with DJC31. These findings reveal the clonal expansion of virulent isolates and connect it to effector diversification that led to resistance breakdown and establish a genomic framework for pathogen surveillance and durable clubroot resistance.
